content.p: Ted Bundy was executed in Florida's electric chair on 24 January 1989, after eleven years of trials, stays and appeals. He was convicted in Utah of kidnapping, and in Florida of three murders: Margaret Bowman and Lisa Levy, killed in a sorority house in Tallahassee, and Kimberly Leach, a 12-year-old schoolgirl from Lake City. The Leach conviction supplied the death warrant that was finally carried out.

In his last days he told detectives from several states about killings elsewhere, and officials have never agreed on how many there were. The New York Times, reporting his death, said investigators believed he had taken 30 or more young women's lives. Everything beyond the three Florida cases rests on his own admissions, which some of the people who heard them doubted, and on investigators' estimates.
content.h2: The 1975 traffic stop and the Utah conviction
content.p: The legal case against Bundy began with a traffic stop. On 16 August 1975 Utah Highway Patrol trooper Bob Hayward pulled over a driver in a suspicious vehicle. ABC4 Utah, reporting Hayward's death in 2017, described that stop as the start of the process that led to Bundy's execution. KSL.com reports that officers searching the car he was driving found handcuffs, a ski mask and pantyhose with eye holes cut out. The Denver Gazette adds an ice pick and a crowbar.

The Seattle Times says he was convicted the following March of kidnapping Carol DaRonch. KSL says Utah court records hold one case under his name, from 1976, for aggravated kidnapping in the second degree over DaRonch's abduction in 1974. She escaped. KSL states that Bundy was never tried or convicted for any murder in Utah.

Later in 1976 he was charged with the murder of Caryn Campbell, a 23-year-old nurse from Michigan who had been on holiday at Snowmass Village, Colorado, in January 1975. The Denver Gazette says a strand of her hair was found in his car, and that her body was discovered in a snowbank near town. He was still awaiting trial in Colorado when he escaped.

Bundy chose to represent himself in the Colorado case, and the Denver Gazette says this gave him access to the law library at the Pitkin County courthouse in Aspen. On 7 June 1977, unshackled and unguarded, he jumped from a second-floor window. By the paper's account he had been gone ten minutes before anyone noticed. A manhunt followed in which vehicles leaving Aspen were searched, and sales of guns and ammunition were halted in nearby towns. Six days later he was reportedly stopped in a stolen car and taken to the Garfield County jail in Glenwood Springs.

On 30 December 1977 he got out again. The Gazette says he had deliberately lost weight to fit through a small opening in the ceiling of his cell, reached the guards' living quarters through the air ducts, changed clothes and walked away. He then made his way to Tallahassee, Florida.

In the early hours of 15 January 1978 someone entered the Chi Omega sorority house at Florida State University. NBC 6 South Florida reports that four women were beaten in their bedrooms. Margaret Bowman, 21, and Lisa Levy, 20, died. Karen Chandler and Kathy Kleiner were badly hurt but recovered. Within the hour, the Eleventh Circuit's later opinion records, another young woman in a nearby house was attacked and survived. NBC identifies her as Cheryl Thomas, who suffered permanent hearing loss.

On 9 February Kimberly Leach disappeared from outside her school in Lake City, Florida. The Deseret News says her body turned up two months later in a pig sty about 35 miles away; NBC 6 says it was found seven weeks later. The Seattle Times describes the place as a deserted hog shed. By the time of his arrest he had been added to the FBI's list of the ten most wanted fugitives, according to the same paper.

The end of his freedom was accidental. In the early hours of 15 February, according to the Seattle Times, Pensacola patrolman David Lee noticed a stolen Volkswagen and signalled it to stop. The driver kicked the officer's legs from under him and ran. Lee fired a warning shot and then a second round, and the two struggled over the officer's gun before Lee made the arrest. It was several days before Pensacola police learned who their car-theft suspect was.

Bundy was indicted for the Chi Omega attacks, and the Deseret News says he tore up the indictment. He pleaded not guilty. Two hours later he was charged with kidnapping and murdering Kimberly Leach. Because an impartial jury could not be found in Tallahassee, the Chi Omega trial was moved to Miami.

The Eleventh Circuit's opinion states that on 24 July 1979 he was convicted of both murders, plus burglary on two counts and attempted first-degree murder on three, and that the judge imposed death sentences for the murders. The Deseret News says he was sentenced to the electric chair a week after the verdict. The Seattle Times reports that bite marks on Levy's body were used to convict him. In his appeals, as the Deseret News summarised them, he challenged the bite-mark evidence and the hypnosis of a witness, and the appeals were eventually denied.

The Leach trial was held in Orlando in 1980. The Deseret News says an Orlando jury deliberated seven hours and 15 minutes before finding him guilty of abducting and murdering her. Bundy acted as his own attorney in that case. During the sentencing hearing in February 1980, the Orlando Sentinel recalled in 1989, he married Carole Boone in a courtroom ceremony after the judge and the jail director had refused her request. He questioned her himself when she took the witness stand to plead for his life, and a notary public witnessed the vows. Shortly afterwards a jury recommended death. NBC 6 says he received the death penalty in both Chi Omega convictions and later a third in the Leach case. The Denver Gazette quotes trial judge Edward Cowart as saying of Bundy's killings that they were "heinous, atrocious and cruel".

The Seattle Times quotes his Chi Omega defence lawyer, Mike Minerva, who said a deal had been worked out in which Bundy would plead guilty to the three Florida killings in exchange for 75 years in prison. According to Minerva, Bundy backed out at the last minute because it meant admitting guilt in front of everyone, which he could not do.

The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the Chi Omega convictions and sentences in June 1984, the Eleventh Circuit records. The United States Supreme Court denied review on 5 May 1986, and on 22 May the governor signed a death warrant, with execution set for 7:00 a.m. on 2 July 1986. State courts finished with his collateral motions on 30 June, and the next day a federal district judge refused a stay and dismissed his habeas petition. The Eleventh Circuit stayed the execution and later reversed that ruling, holding that the district court had erred in denying a stay and in dismissing the petition, and sending the case back for careful consideration. The Deseret News says the appeals court and later the Supreme Court ultimately rejected his appeal.

The New York Times counted the final order as the fourth death warrant signed by a Florida governor; three had been issued in 1986 and stayed while courts heard his claims. The Deseret News adds that prison authorities thwarted an escape attempt, finding a loose bar and hacksaw blades. Governor Bob Martinez signed the last warrant on 17 January 1989. Martinez later told the Seattle Times that the following seven days were hectic, with Bundy and his lawyer trying different angles to avoid the sentence.
content.h2: The last week and the confessions
content.p: Through his trials Bundy maintained his innocence. Journalists Stephen Michaud and Hugh Aynesworth interviewed him on death row in 1980, and Michaud said he never confessed to them. Oxygen quotes FBI agent Bill Hagmaier as saying that Bundy, in his earlier talks with the bureau, did not admit to killing anyone, and that his confessions came in the final days. Hagmaier said their purpose was to "extend his life", and Bundy's lawyer Polly Nelson said he believed that offering to confess would make the governor delay the execution by a few years.

The New York Times said detectives from Washington, Utah, Idaho and Colorado travelled to the prison and that Bundy confessed to at least 16 killings in the last days. Philly.com reported at least 20 murders confessed in Western states during the previous three days. Oxygen reports that Bundy admitted to 30 murders, telling Hagmaier "I think that's a fairly close figure." Britannica says he ultimately confessed to 28.

The numbers did not hold together. On 22 January Salt Lake County investigator Dennis Couch spent about 90 minutes with him. KSL reports that Bundy later told Washington state investigators he had killed eight women in Utah, that Utah authorities quickly ruled out three of those, and that police a month after his death could pin only five killings on him. Of the five women police believed he killed in Utah, only the bodies of two, Melissa Smith and Laura Ann Aime, were recovered. Couch described him as "defeated" and so tired that he nearly fell asleep. Author Ann Rule, who had known Bundy, said she believed he gave Utah police false burial locations as a scheme to send them "slopping through the mud in vain".

Washington investigator Bob Keppel also recorded interviews. A transcript released shortly before the Deseret News reported on it on 2 April 1989 shows Bundy describing the abduction of Georgann Hawkins, who vanished from behind a University of Washington sorority in June 1974, and saying he had approached another woman at the same sorority and then abandoned the attempt. A forensic psychologist who had worked on his appeals, Art Norman, told the Oregonian that Bundy told him his first victims were two women in the Philadelphia area around 1969. Philadelphia police began checking unsolved cases but found none immediately linked to him, and a New Jersey State Police lieutenant said Bundy was not a suspect in any case there.

On Monday 23 January, the Times reported, he tearfully told the religious broadcaster James Dobson that hard-core pornography had become an obsession that drove him. Rule called that meeting a "con game". According to Hagmaier, who spoke to him on the last night, Bundy talked of suicide, saying he would not give the state the pleasure of watching him die, and that he asked to rehearse the execution.

Bundy was strapped into the chair at Florida State Prison and told his lawyer and a minister, "Give my love to my family and friends." Prison officials said 2,000 volts passed through his body for one minute, and he was pronounced dead at 7:16 a.m. The Times said about 200 people outside the gates cheered when the signal came. Jerry Blair, the prosecutor in the Leach trial, who watched as a witness, said he and others who had worked the case were no closer to knowing what turned Bundy into a killer.

Assistant state attorney Bob Dekle, who had helped convict Bundy of Leach's murder, remembered the scene where the child's body was found. "I kept thinking that's where it started. This is where it ends," he said, adding a decade later that for people such as Kimberly Leach's family it would never be over.

Questions that the confessions did not settle remain open. The Seattle Times noted in 1999 that the FBI said he had killed more than 30 women, while Keppel, the Washington investigator, said no human remains had been found, though investigators felt he had committed the murders he confessed to. Britannica notes that some have estimated hundreds of deaths. The only killings for which a court found him responsible were the three in Florida.
